The dragon did not move.

Neither did I.

That seemed fair for the first few seconds.

Then it became his choice.

I had just told a creature older than my kingdom that the future he remembered me not being part of had happened with me in it once already.

There were several reasonable responses to that.

Disbelief.

Questions.

Eating me.

I had prepared for two of those.

Ithar stared.

I shifted my weight off the bad leg.

The movement was small.

His eye followed it anyway.

There was no body language to wait out.

Slow and steady.

“You are sixty soon. Your species measures a life in decades and then behaves surprised when there are not enough of them. You are not surprised. That interests me.

“You have been searching for me for years. You have already lived two lives by your own description. You arrived with enough food to reach me, not enough to return comfortably. Your planning prioritizes arrival over departure.

“I do not know what conclusion belongs to those facts yet. I know only that they belong in the account.”

A woman's hand.

A child's laugh.

A wooden leg leaning against a bed because the socket had rubbed the skin raw that day.

I stopped there.

Not yet.

Ithar's nostril moved.

He had heard the silence change again.

This time the question was small enough to deserve being spoken.

“Where does the discrepancy begin?”

I looked at him.

“Nineteen.”

The dragon held my eyes.

“Begin there.”

I rested my hands on my knees.

Both of them felt old.

Only one had been old the first time.

“Fine.”

Young skin.

At nineteen, the first time, I had gone to Guild Hall and registered for field work.

Three weeks later I took the ridge contract because it paid nearly double local rate.

Six months later I could reinforce my legs without vomiting.

Four years later I crossed the western cuts with people who taught me things no hall instructor ever had.

Twenty-one years later I wore an S on my badge.

There were seven of us that year.

captures.transcript:
Roads closed during pressure work. Temporary barriers. Contractors complaining about lost hours. Stations humming under stone. The Line so ordinary I had spent most of my first life treating it like weather.

At fifty-nine, people were going to die because we had treated it like weather.

At nineteen, someone on this street swore because the maintenance bell meant his cart would be late.

I laughed.

The woman in the blue coat looked at me.

I kept walking.

Guild Hall was three districts over.

Then I threw up one more time.

Less impressive.

By the time I reached Guild Hall, I had mud on one boot and a sour taste in my mouth.

The building looked exactly as terrible as I remembered.

Long stone front. Narrow windows. Three lines outside before the doors even opened.

Field registry on the left.

Trade certification in the middle.

Contract labor on the right.

At nineteen the first time, I had looked at those doors and felt like my life was about to begin.

I took a new sheet.

The woman had a brass name strip that said MIRA.

I knew her.

Not well.

In my first life she had worked that window for at least twelve years. By the time I reached B-class she had moved upstairs and developed the rare administrative power to make senior Rankers wait in chairs.

She had once made me wait forty minutes because I called a renewal requirement stupid.

It had been stupid.

She had still won.

I used black ink.

Name.

Age.

District.

Previous certification.

Cheap brass pretending to be something else.

“On this? Enough that the answer doesn't matter.”

His mouth tightened.

“Assume standard Line bronze.”

I gave him the number.

He looked at me again.

This time longer.

“Where did you learn that?”

I had several answers available.

Most were bad.

“Work.”

“What work?”

“Family.”

Also bad.

My father repaired mill housings. He knew pressure fittings, but not that number.

The examiner glanced at my form.

“No prior certification.”

“Informal.”

A foreman named Kett who lied about hazard pay and taught me how to sleep through blasting.

The first reinforcement drill I learned correctly from a woman whose name I could no longer remember.

The broken wrist.

The fever.

The winter extension nobody had mentioned.

The first time I killed something large enough that people stopped treating me like a boy.

The first time somebody died because I was not fast enough.

The road from there to S-class was not straight.

It existed.

He walked toward the clerk desk without looking back.

I stood there waiting to feel smarter.

Mostly I felt unemployed.

“Good start,” I muttered.

The local board had worse money.

That was offensive in a more familiar way.

Six silver for warehouse security.

Five for cart escort inside the district, which barely counted as leaving home.

Seven for night vermin clearing under the east market.

Eight for Line auxiliary maintenance.

I stopped.

LINE AUXILIARY MAINTENANCE, EAST DISTRICT.

The first time I had been nineteen, I chose twelve silver and a road that helped turn me into the man I remembered.

The second time I chose eight and a station I had barely noticed.

I told myself it was temporary.

That mattered.

If I had admitted I was changing the route, I might have been more careful about what changing meant.

Instead I told myself I was improving it.

I knew the expensive lessons already.

I did not need the broken wrist.

I did not need Kett's bad stew.

I sighed.

Dera's expression changed.

I knew that face from both sides.

“Replace the housing,” she repeated.

The woman beside me closed her eyes.

Not dramatically.

Why did I remember the stew?

The stew had carrots.

At first.

The summer heat made the upper housings unbearable.

Two crews hated each other over a tool cabinet nobody remembered buying.

Dera had the emotional range of a door when she was tired, which was often.

Nessa could hold a grudge through three meals and then forget what started it.

I got pressure burns on both forearms because I trusted a gauge I knew had been wrong last week and somehow decided that made it honest this week.

I went home angry.

My mother told me I smelled like a hot spoon.

“Oh.”

“What?”

By then I knew every sound East Four made when it was healthy.

I knew which pipes sweated before rain.

Which floor drain backed up when the market washed fish waste at the wrong hour.

Which valve needed a kick and which one would remove a foot if you tried.

Three people died and what survived in my memory was traffic.

I looked closer.

The tie-in point had been moved two meters east from the original station mark.

“Who approved this?”

Dera pointed to a seal.

“District engineering.”

“Who there?”

“Halden.”

I knew the name.

Not personally.

From the black board.

One of the dead men had been an engineer.

I felt cold in a room that was never cold.

Nessa noticed.

“What?”

“The chamber can't take that angle.”

Dera looked at the plan.

“That puts it under the old market drain,” Nessa said.

“Yes.”

“Which floods.”

“Yes.”

“Every spring.”

Halden rubbed his eyes.

I liked him immediately.

Not because he was brilliant.

Because when presented with evidence that his plan was wrong, he became tired instead of proud.

captures.transcript:
For one beautiful second I thought I had fixed history.

Then every relief bell in East Four rang at once.

Nessa looked at me.

“What did you do?”

“Wrong thing.”

The lower floor jumped.

Not shook.

Jumped.

Stone lifted under my boots.

The room moved sideways.

Someone screamed.

Steam hit the far wall.

A bronze line tore loose and swung across the chamber hard enough to cut a railing in half.

Nessa was on the wrong side of it.

I did not think.

That part was still S-class.

The paint cracked around a circular seam.

Old load mark underneath.

Very old.

The same family of mark Ithar later pulled from his hoard.

I did not know that yet.

I knew enough.

We vented the buried chamber.

East Four survived.

So did everyone inside it.

Seven people were injured.

Two badly.

No deaths.

I spent the night in a healer's ward with burns across my back and a left shoulder that would click before rain for the rest of that body.

Nessa woke six beds away.

“Separate motive from method. Wanting her alive does not make the method correct. Surviving the mistake does not make the motive foolish. What did the difference teach you?”

I looked at my right hand.

The two fingers that did not close properly now had nothing to do with East Four.

The leg did not either.

Life had plenty left to take.

But the shoulder did.

A little piece of that day had stayed all the way to the mountain.

“Knowing what happens isn't the same as knowing why.”

captures.transcript:
I almost left East Four in the seventh year.

Not because I was unhappy.

That would have been easier.

Unhappy people are allowed to leave.

Happy people have to explain themselves.

The offer came from the Guild in a red envelope.

Red meant hazard authority.

It also meant money.

Enough money that Nessa read the number twice.

“That's monthly?”

“Weekly.”

She looked at me.

“Fuck you.”

“I didn't set it.”

“Read it again.”

I did.

She took the letter.

Western Corridor Recovery.

I knew how to sleep in armor.

I knew what a body sounded like when reinforcement failed from the inside.

I had been climbing.

Always.

You take the better contract.

Then the harder one.

Then somebody notices.

Then the work changes because now they know you can survive it.

Then you survive that too.

“You're doing the face again,” Nessa said.

“What face?”

“Arguing with someone who isn't here.”

“Maybe he's here.”

She looked around the room.

“Then he's cheap and not paying rent.”

I laughed.

The letter moved under my thumb.

“What do you want?” she asked.

I hated the question immediately.

“Six months isn't forever.”

“That wasn't what I asked.”

“You and my father need new questions.”

“Your father is smarter than you.”

“Unfortunately.”

“What do you want?”

I looked at the letter.

captures.transcript:
That pissed me off.

Not because tables are profound.

Because they are not.

I had spent years becoming someone who thought important choices should feel important.

Dragons.

Monsters.

S-class contracts.

People dying.

A kingdom failing.

A table had no business in the decision.

Neither did peaches.

Or a roof leak.

Or my father's carrots.

Or whether my nephew learned my name before I left for six months.

That was the problem.

Life kept refusing to organize itself by importance.

I knew when he was about to ask for a tool.

I knew he hated people standing behind his right shoulder.

I knew he drank coffee black when tired and ruined it with sugar when scared.

I knew the little line beside his mouth meant he was about to disagree with Dera and was trying to decide how much employment he needed.

He knew none of that about me.

Once he reached for a wrench without looking.

I put the correct one in his hand.

He paused.

Looked at it.

Then at me.

“Good guess.”

“Yeah.”

“North breach survey. Authority closed the contract. No rupture.”

I took the bulletin.

My hands were suddenly cold.

The North Vey rupture happened when I was twenty-seven the first time.

It killed eighty-six people.

Bren and I had been there after.

Not during the first break.

After.

We spent eleven days clearing tunnels.

That was where his ankle got crushed.

That was where the scar above his right eye came from.

That was where he advanced to A-class.

captures.transcript:
First life, I had known exactly how strong it was.

I had watched it shake.

I had seen blood between those fingers.

I had held that hand when he died because neither of us knew what else to do with the last minute.

Second life, it was just a hand offered by a man leaving a station.

I took it.

“You too.”

He left.

I did not follow.

The cave returned softly around me.

I opened my eyes.

Ithar was quiet for long enough that the silence itself became the question.

Then he took the floor.
